transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Well... honestly, what brings me in is that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. I've been a carpenter for, gosh, almost forty years now, right out of high school, and I've always worked in a busy shop. But lately, it's like every little thing pulls me away. 

I'll be right in the middle of measuring out a cut for a set of cabinets, and... well, say one saw starts up on the other side of the shop. Just a regular saw, nothing I haven't heard a million times before, but my brain just snaps to it and I lose my place. Or somebody will walk past the office window, and I just have to stop what I'm doing to see who it is and where they're going. 

And it's not even just the noise or the people around me, it's my own head, too. I'll be right in the middle of a task, totally hands-on, and a thought about another job we're doing will just pop up out of nowhere, and it completely pulls me off what I’m doing. I'll put my tools down to go check on the materials for that other job, and then I start doing something over there, and then... well, then the whole day just gets away from me. I look at the clock and it's suddenly quitting time, and I haven't actually finished the one thing I originally set out to do. It’s just so incredibly frustrating because I have work to get done and I just can't seem to stay on track.
Would you say this kind of distractibility is something you've dealt with on and off since you were young, or is this a new change from how your mind used to work?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, I was just talking to my sister about this the other day, actually. We were going through some old boxes of our mother's things—she passed a few years ago, bless her heart—and we found a whole stack of my old report cards from grade school. And looking at them, it was just... well, it was like reading a story about someone else, but also exactly about me, if that makes sense? 

Even back then, way before I was even twelve, probably starting in second or third grade, the teachers were writing the exact same things. Every single year, it was always, "She's a bright girl, but she's so careless." And I remember my mother getting so frustrated with me because I would constantly lose my homework. I mean, I'd do it—sometimes, anyway—and then I'd just leave it on the kitchen table, or it would get crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack, or I'd just flat-out forget what the instructions were by the time I got home. 

And the teachers, they always complained that I was staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. I remember Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, she had this big classroom right next to the playground, and I would just sit there watching the leaves blow around or looking at the older kids playing kickball, completely forgetting that I had a whole sheet of math problems in front of me. So, I guess... I guess what I'm saying is, it's not entirely new. It's just that now, it feels so much more... I don't know, severe? Like, back then, the worst that happened was I got a bad grade or a talking-to from my mom. But now, it's my livelihood, you know? It's the cabinets I'm building, the jobs I'm supposed to be finishing. But the way my mind just drifts off... yeah, it's been doing that since I was a little girl. I just never really thought about it being connected until I saw those old report cards.
Aside from the distractibility, do you notice things like feeling restless or fidgety, having trouble sitting still, or often interrupting others and blurting things out?

Well, no, not the interrupting so much. I've always been pretty good about letting folks finish their piece, you know? But the sitting still... oh, boy, that's a whole other story. 

See, in the shop, I'm always on my feet, moving from the saw to the workbench, grabbing clamps, hauling lumber. So I never really noticed it as a problem until recently. But, well, I had this spill a few months back—just tripped over an extension cord that some new kid left stretched across the floor, which is a huge safety hazard, by the way, and I told the foreman as much—but anyway, I took a tumble and sprained my wrist pretty bad. So they had me on light duty for a while, which meant sitting at the desk in the back office, doing material estimates and going over blueprints, or sitting through these incredibly long production meetings that just seem to drag on and on forever. 

And I'm telling you, Dr. Lee, it was absolute torture. If I have to sit at that desk doing estimates or sit through a long meeting, I feel this... this awful, tight feeling, like I'm just completely wound up inside. It's like my legs have a mind of their own and they're just screaming at me to get up and move around, to pace the floor, to go check on something, anything! And the worst part is, my wrist is pretty much healed up now, and I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork because it's part of the job, especially as you get older and they want you doing more of the planning side of things. But I just can't stand it. I'll be sitting there, tapping my foot, shifting in my chair a hundred times, picking up a pen and putting it down, just feeling like a coiled spring that's about to snap. I literally have to force myself to stay in the chair, and even then, I usually end up finding some excuse to get up and walk to the breakroom for water, just to relieve that jittery feeling inside my chest. It's exhausting, honestly, just trying to make myself sit still like a normal person.
Do you notice this same restlessness and trouble focusing affecting you outside of work too—like at home, during conversations, or when you're trying to relax or do errands?

Oh, gosh, yes. It’s not just at the shop, not by a long shot. It’s... well, it’s everywhere, honestly. Take being at home, for instance. You’d think after a long day of standing on concrete floors and hauling wood around, I’d just want to sink into my recliner and not move a muscle, right? But even when I'm supposed to be relaxing, or when things are just supposed to be... you know, quiet... I just can't do it. My husband, bless him, he likes to watch those long historical documentaries in the evenings, the ones where the narrator speaks real slow and not much is happening? And I try, I really try to sit there with him, but I catch myself tapping my foot against the coffee table, or shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, over and over. 

And then there's church! Oh my goodness, Dr. Lee, church is probably the hardest part of my entire week. We go to this lovely church down the road, been going there for twenty years, and the pastor is a wonderful man, he really is, but during the sermon, or especially during the silent prayer... it is just agonizing. When things are supposed to be quiet like that, I feel this absolute need to move. I’ll start whispering to my husband about what we’re having for lunch, or I'm digging around in my purse, or I’ll just get up and walk to the restroom for absolutely no real reason other than the fact that sitting still in that quiet feels almost unbearable. 

It’s like the quieter the room is, the louder that jittery feeling gets inside me. My husband is always giving me that little sideways look, you know the one, gently putting his hand on my knee to get me to stop bouncing my leg. So, yes, it definitely follows me home. final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a longstanding, pervasive pattern (since early elementary school, prior to age 12) of significant inattentive symptoms (distractibility by external stimuli and internal thoughts, difficulty sustaining task focus, forgetfulness, careless errors noted by teachers) combined with prominent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to remain seated, subjective restlessness, fidgeting, need to move in quiet settings) across multiple settings (work, home, church). Both symptom domains are currently present, longstanding, and functionally impairing, meeting criteria for ADHD Combined Presentation (F90.2) rather than predominantly inattentive (F90.0) or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive (F90.1) type.
